title: Tsadi Hebrew Letter (צ): Tzaddi, Sound & Final Tsadi
description: Learn the Hebrew letter Tsadi (צ), also spelled Tzaddi or Tsade: its [ts] sound, final Tsadi (ץ), words like צֵל (shadow) and interactive practice.

blocks.text: Tsadi Hebrew Letter (צ): Sound, Final Tsadi & Practice

Tsadi (צ) is the eighteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. In modern Hebrew, it represents [ts], like the joined ts sound in English 'cats'. Tsadi has two written forms: the regular form צ and the final form ץ, called Tsadi Sofit. They are forms of the same letter, not two separate letters of the alphabet.
Tsadi Sofit (ץ) is the final form of Tsadi. It represents the same [ts] sound as צ, like ts in 'cats'.

illustration.label: Tsadi Sofit
illustration.equivalent: Final Tsadi: Tsadi with its stem extended straight down below the line, written at the end of a word and pronounced [ts].

blocks.text: In ordinary Hebrew words, the regular form צ appears at the beginning or in the middle, and Tsadi Sofit (ץ) appears at the end. 'Sofit' means 'final'. Both forms represent [ts]. A dagesh in Tsadi does not require a doubled consonant in ordinary modern Hebrew.

The Hebrew word 'צַיִד' [tsa-yid] means 'hunting'. It has three letters: Tsadi (צ), Yud (י), and Dalet (ד). The Patah (ַ) beneath Tsadi gives [a], making [tsa]. Yud with a Hiriq (ִ) gives [yi], and Dalet closes the second syllable with [d]. Say two syllables, tsa-yid, with the stress on tsa. Do not add a vowel after the final d.

The Hebrew word 'צֵל' [tsel] means 'shadow'. It has two letters: Tsadi (צ) and Lamed (ל). The Tsere (ֵ) beneath Tsadi gives [e], and Lamed gives [l]. Say tsel as one syllable, with a steady e; no special vowel length is required.

The Hebrew word 'חֵפֶץ' [che-fets] means 'object', a physical thing. It has three letters: Chet (ח), Pey (פ), and Tsadi Sofit (ץ). Chet with a Tsere gives [che], with the throaty ch of 'loch'. Pey without a dagesh gives [f], and its Segol (ֶ) gives [e]. Tsadi Sofit gives the final [ts]. Say two syllables, che-fets, with the stress on che. Both vowels are [e]; the different vowel signs do not require a difference in length in modern Hebrew.

Read each word aloud. גַּן [gan], 'garden', has one syllable. בִּטָּחוֹן [bi-ta-chon], 'security', has three syllables, with the stress on chon; the dagesh in Tet does not require a doubled t in modern Hebrew. מְהֵרָה [me-he-ra], 'quickly', is a literary word: in this careful reading, the initial Sheva is read as e, giving three syllables with the stress on ra; a reduced two-syllable reading, [mhe-ra], is also used. אָבַד [a-vad] means 'he/it was lost', a past-tense verb form; it has two syllables, with the stress on vad. פּוֹעַל [po-al] means 'verb' in grammar; it has two syllables, with the stress on po. Keep o and a separate. Also review חֶבֶל [che-vel], 'rope': two syllables, with the stress on che. In חֶבֶל, Bet without a dagesh gives [v].

You have practised Tsadi (צ), the eighteenth letter, and its final form, Tsadi Sofit (ץ). Both represent [ts], like ts in 'cats'. Tsadi is the last of the five letters with a final form in alphabetical order. Now test your reading and understanding of the words in this lesson.

exercises.prompt: What sound does the letter Tsadi (צ) make?
exercises.explanation: Think of the joined ts sound at the end of 'cats'.

exercises.prompt: The letter Tsadi (צ) has a final form called Tsadi Sofit (ץ).
exercises.explanation: Tsadi Sofit (ץ) is the final form of the same letter, Tsadi (צ).

exercises.prompt: Match the Hebrew words with their English meanings.
exercises.explanation: צֵל [tsel] means 'shadow'; חֵפֶץ [che-fets] means 'object'; צַיִד [tsa-yid] means 'hunting'.

exercises.prompt: How many forms of Tsadi are used in ordinary Hebrew words?
exercises.explanation: Tsadi has two forms: the regular form (צ) and the final form (ץ).

exercises.prompt: In ordinary Hebrew words, Tsadi Sofit (ץ) can appear in the middle of a word.
exercises.explanation: Use the regular form צ in the middle and Tsadi Sofit (ץ) at the end.
צַיִד is [tsa-yid], 'hunting': two syllables, with the stress on tsa. The final d belongs to yid.

exercises.prompt: What vowel sound does Segol (ֶ) represent in צֶ?
exercises.explanation: Segol represents [e], roughly as in 'bet'. With Tsadi [ts], it makes [tse].

exercises.prompt: Tsadi Sofit (ץ) is pronounced differently from the regular Tsadi (צ).
exercises.explanation: Both forms represent [ts], like ts in 'cats'.

exercises.prompt: Match the English words with their Hebrew equivalents.
exercises.explanation: חֶבֶל means 'rope', צֵל means 'shadow', and פּוֹעַל means 'verb' in grammar.

exercises.prompt: What is the meaning of the Hebrew word חֵפֶץ?
exercises.explanation: חֵפֶץ [che-fets] means 'object', a physical thing. Stress the first syllable, che.

exercises.prompt: How is the word פּוֹעַל pronounced?
exercises.explanation: פּוֹעַל [po-al] means 'verb' in grammar. Say two syllables, with the stress on po; keep o and a separate.

exercises.prompt: In ordinary Hebrew words, Tsadi Sofit (ץ) is used only at the end of a word.
exercises.explanation: Tsadi Sofit (ץ) is the final form; the regular form צ is used at the beginning or in the middle.

exercises.prompt: How is the word חֶבֶל pronounced?
exercises.explanation: חֶבֶל [che-vel] means 'rope'. Say two syllables, with the stress on che; ch is the throaty sound in 'loch'.

exercises.prompt: Match each letter form to its sound and, for Tsadi, its position in a word.
exercises.explanation: In text with vowel points, פ without a dagesh represents [f]. Both צ and ץ represent [ts]; regular צ appears at the beginning or in the middle, and final ץ at the end.

exercises.prompt: In ordinary modern Hebrew, Tsadi is pronounced [ts] without a required doubling.
exercises.explanation: A dagesh in Tsadi does not require you to pronounce a doubled consonant in ordinary modern Hebrew.
